usurp

yoo-SURP · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To usurp is to take a position of power or authority illegally or by force.

The ambitious duke waited for the king's coronation to be delayed so he could usurp the crown himself.

Example

While the elected chairperson was on medical leave, her deputy quietly usurped control of the committee, changing bylaws no one had voted on.

The deputy didn't wait for a proper vote or transition -- he seized authority that wasn't legitimately his while no one was watching. That illegitimate power grab is exactly what usurp describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

seize: To seize is to grab something suddenly and forcibly, and the word is neutral about right and wrong -- police can seize evidence lawfully. To usurp is never neutral: it means taking a position or power that rightfully belongs to someone else, so the taking is illegitimate by definition.

commandeer: To commandeer is to take charge of a thing -- a truck, a boat, a building -- usually for temporary use in an urgent situation. To usurp is about titles and authority rather than objects: a throne, an office, or a role is taken from the person it rightfully belongs to.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

relinquish: to voluntarily give up power, control, or possession

inherit: to receive a position or property through a legitimate, established process

Where it sits · how wrongfully power is taken

assume → usurp → overthrow

assume vs. usurp: To assume a role can be entirely proper -- a milder act than to usurp, since assuming can happen with everyone's approval, while to usurp is always a wrongful taking of a position that belongs to someone else.

overthrow vs. usurp: To overthrow a government is an even more dramatic, often violent removal of power than usurping a single position.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — usu-: by use, through use (Latin (usus))

root — -rp (rapere): to seize, to snatch (Latin)

Put it together: Usurp comes from Latin usus ('use') + rapere ('to seize') -- roughly 'to seize for one's own use.' It came to mean grabbing a position of power that rightfully belongs to someone else.

Use the root in a new word: rapt: In the old fable, the rapacious wolf finally meets his match.

Root Check

Word Choice

Usurp is a strong political or historical word for an illegitimate power grab -- it's rarely used for winning something through a fair contest, election, or agreed-upon process. Compare it with subjugate, which describes conquering an entire people or group, while usurp usually targets one specific position or title.
